tier_reason: Upgraded from C. Source is Delving Bitcoin topic 2087 (Nov 2025) by Sebastian Falbesoner (theStack). It uses a public harness, github.com/theStack/secp256k1-plugbench. build_libs.sh pins the exact libsecp256k1 commits used in Bitcoin Core v0.12 through v30.0 and the OpenSSL tags 0.9.8h, 1.0.0, 1.1.1, 3.0.0, 3.1.0, 3.3.0 and 3.5.0, all as default shared builds. secp-plugbench.c dlopens each .so and times, with CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID, pubkey parse + DER signature parse + ECDSA verify over 5000 signatures made with libsecp256k1. The OpenSSL path uses EC_GROUP_precompute_mult. Three runs have results. (1) The author on an arm64 machine with gcc 14.2.0 reports >8x (first-party). (2) Pieter Wuille on a Ryzen 5950X with 500000 iterations reports 8.5x (first-party; compiler not stated). (3) Bayernatoor, an independent third party with 0 commits in bitcoin-core/secp256k1, reproduced it in plugbench issue #2 on an AMD Ryzen 9 3950X with gcc 12.2.0 on Debian x86_64 (chart only, about 9.0x). Falbesoner and Wuille are both listed in secp256k1 SECURITY.md (maintainer keys), so they are first-party. The A criteria are met: public code, a stated compiler, default flags fixed by the public build script, and a stated CPU. Run 3 meets all of them and is independent. Run 1 lacks only the CPU model.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ECDSA verify on secp256k1 (compressed-pubkey parse + DER sig parse + verify), libsecp256k1 at Bitcoin Core v30.0 (v0.7.0, commit b9313c6) vs OpenSSL 3.5.0. Ryzen 9 5950X (Wuille): 8.5x (stated). Author's arm64 with gcc 14.2.0: '>8x' stated, about 8.3x read from the chart. Ryzen 9 3950X with gcc 12.2.0 (independent issue #2): about 9.0x read from the chart. Historical baseline, libsecp at Core v0.12 (2015) vs OpenSSL 1.1.1: about 4.3x (arm64), 5.4x (5950X) and 4.8x (3950X), read from the charts. The original PR #6954 claim was 2.5-5.5x. Chart readings are pixel measurements, accurate to about ±2-3%.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler: gcc 14.2.0 for the author's arm64 run and gcc 12.2.0 for the independent 3950X run. Wuille's 5950X run does not state a compiler. All builds use defaults with no custom flags. libsecp256k1 was built with ./autogen.sh && ./configure --enable-static=no --enable-benchmark=no --enable-tests=no --enable-exhaustive-tests=no && make, which gives autoconf '-g -O2' plus libsecp's own -O2 (checked in the v0.7.0 configure.ac). OpenSSL was built with ./config shared && make, whose Linux release default is -O3 (checked in 3.5.0 Configurations/10-main.conf). The harness itself is built with plain cc. These are not Bitcoin Core's own build flags.
corrections.hardware: Author: unnamed arm64 machine (he says 3 machines gave very similar results). Wuille: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X. Independent: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 32GB RAM, Debian x86_64.
corrections.caveats: The two headline runs (>8x and 8.5x) are first-party: both are listed in libsecp256k1 SECURITY.md. The only independent run is a GitHub issue with a chart and no stated ratio. OpenSSL's secp256k1 path is not specially optimized (the post notes P-256 is heavily optimized, and OpenSSL PR #26097 aims to speed up secp256k1), so this comparison does not show OpenSSL is slow in general. The harness uses the deprecated EC_KEY/o2i_ECPublicKey/ECDSA_verify API. Each run times the 5000 signatures once by default; Wuille used 500000 iterations because of run-to-run variance. OpenSSL 0.9.8h and 1.0.0 crash on arm64 and were skipped. Old libsecp versions were built with modern compilers, which biases the history (Wuille). Arch-dependent: bc-22.0 safegcd gave about 30% on arm64, -3.6% on the 5950X and about 16% on the 3950X, and bc-27.0 (x86_64 asm removal) gave +8% on the 5950X. The harness repo has no license. The archive file is on branch 'master', not 'main'.
